Jazz Theory: Practice for Chapter 31

Exercises for Chapter 31 of Hutchinson’s Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom: writing and naming jazz chords by the book’s symbol rules, altered dominants, guide tones, hearing chord qualities, ii–V–I and turnarounds played by the band with tritone substitutions, the book’s scales and chord-scale relationships.

This page goes with Chapter 31, Introduction to Jazz Theory of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Read each section there first; the book is the reference for the terms and symbol rules used here. It builds on the seventh chords of Chapter 8 and the ii–V–I of Chapter 9.

Every drill has Settings, and is also on the Theory Drills page. The band demos play with ▶ Play; the strip at the bottom of the page shows the bar.

Typing chord symbols: as the book writes them, with b and # for ♭ and ♯. Δ can be typed maj, M or ^; minor as m, min or -; half-diminished as ø, h or m7b5; diminished as °, o or dim. Parentheses are optional: C7(#9b5), C7#9b5 and C7(♯9♭5) are the same.

31.1 Jazz chord basics

The book’s ground rules for jazz chord symbols:

  • Every number up to the highest is there. C9 has the 7th as well; C13 is C E G B♭ D F A, everything up to the 13th. So for C E G B♭ D A (no 11th) the book writes C9(13). Players write C13 for that chord and leave out the clashing 11th, but the book is exact.
  • 9, 11 and 13 are major or perfect (from the major scale) unless marked: 9 is the 2nd an octave up, 11 the 4th, 13 the 6th.
  • Δ or maj applies to the 7th: CΔ9 is a major 7th chord with a 9th, not a “major 9th”. m or – applies to the 3rd.
  • + and – before 5, 9, 11 or 13 mean ♯ and ♭. C+7 is an augmented triad with a minor 7th.
  • “add 9” when there is a 9th but no 7th; 6/9 when there are a 6th and a 9th (C6/9 = C E G A D).
  • The minor-major 7th (mΔ7) is common in jazz too.
  • Double sharps and flats get respelled (and sometimes B♯, C♭, E♯, F♭), the way a pianist would think of them.
  • The bass is the root here; slash chords come later. Read 31.1

31.2 Chord symbol specifics

Three rules for choosing between names:

  • 6 or 13: call it 6 only without a 7th. With a 7th, it is 13.
  • 11 or sus: sus (the 4th) replaces the 3rd. With a 3rd present, the 4th is an 11. C7sus is C F G B♭.
  • ♭5 or ♯11: with an ordinary 5th in the chord, F♯ over C is ♯11. Without one, either name is fine. Read 31.2

The drills follow these rules when they check a name. A name is right when it means the same notes over the same root. A 5th the chord leaves out is fine: C9 counts for C E B♭ D.

31.3 Altered dominant 7ths

A dominant 7th is altered when its 5th or 9th is raised or lowered (or both). The root, 3rd and 7th never change. - ♯5 may be written as ♭6 on the staff (G♯ or A♭ over C), to agree with the ♭7. - ♯9 is usually written as a ♭10 (E♭ over C), so the chord seems to have both a major and minor 3rd. It is still not a minor chord: ♭11 isn’t used, because that note is the major 3rd. - The book prefers ♯5 to ♭13. ♭13 means the 5th is there too; ♯5 means it isn’t. - 7alt says the 5th and 9th are altered without saying how, so it doesn’t name exact notes. - Dominants are usually altered when they work as dominants, resolving down a 5th, and usually left plain when they are the tonic, as in the first chord of a blues. Read 31.3

Write the altered dominants. Either spelling of ♯5 and ♯9 counts, as the book allows:

The book’s list of chords, condensed from The New Real Book, shown on C. The drills use exactly these:

Group Chords (on C)

Sus chords Csus · C7sus · C9sus · C13sus · C7sus(♭9) · C13sus(♭9)
Altered dominants C7(♭5) · C7(♯5) · C7(♭9) · C7(♯9) · C7(♯9♭5) · C7(♯9♯5) · C7(♭9♯5) · C7(♭9♭5)
Other CmΔ7 · CmΔ9 · Cdim · C°7 · Cdim(Δ7) · C7(♯11♯9)

Read 31.4

31.5 Writing jazz chords

Start from all the major and perfect notes up to the 13th (1 3 5 7 9 11 13: on D, D F♯ A C♯ E G B). Keep what the symbol’s highest number includes, then change what the symbol changes. DmΔ11: minor 3rd, major 7th, then 9 and 11, so D F A C♯ E G. E7(♯11♯9♯5): E G♯ B D, then ♯5 (B♯, written C to agree with the D), ♯9 (F𝄪, written G) and ♯11 (A♯, or B♭). Read 31.5

31.6 Analysing jazz chords

The same scratch-paper method in reverse. Write all the major and perfect notes up to the 13th on the bass note. Compare, and work out, in order: 1. the quality of the 7th chord; 2. the upper notes (9, 11, 13); 3. what is altered; 4. what may be respelled.

Two checks from the book’s examples: - Spot the sus. With no 3rd but a 4th, the chord is sus, and the 4th isn’t also an 11. - 5ths are often left out. Read 31.6

31.7 Guide tones and voicings

The guide tones are a chord’s 3rd and 7th: they decide its quality. In a progression by fifths (ii–V–I, iii–vi–ii–V), each guide tone moves by a half or whole step, or stays put. Below, dominant 7ths go round the circle of fifths: the bass plays the roots and the right hand plays only the 3rd and 7th. Each chord’s 3rd becomes the next one’s 7th, and each 7th falls a half step to the next 3rd. The engraving is this site’s, of the exercise the book describes:

Two chords a tritone apart (C7 and F♯7) share the same guide tones, swapped: that is what makes the tritone substitution in 31.8 work. Read 31.7

Name the guide tones of each chord:

The book’s voicings have five notes. In close voicings, the root is in the left hand and the other four sit close together in the right, with the 3rd or the 7th lowest. In spread voicings, the root, 3rd and 7th are lowest, with the other notes above them, often a 4th or 5th apart. (A sus chord’s 4th takes the 3rd’s place; a 6th takes the 7th’s.) This drill plays close voicings. Name the quality by ear: listen to the guide tones first.

31.8 Standard progressions

ii–V–I

The most common progression in jazz. The book’s examples are “Autumn Leaves”, “What Is This Thing Called Love”, “Tune-Up”, “Pent Up House”, “Lady Bird” and “Firm Roots”. In major the book voices it Dm9 – G9(13) – CΔ9, in minor Dm7(♭5) – G7alt – Cm6/9. The band plays both. (The band’s chord symbols are written its own way; it plays a 13 chord without the 11th, as players do.)

Type the ii–V–I in each key. Any usual version counts: Dm7, Dm9 or Dm11; any dominant on V; CΔ7, CΔ9, C6 or C6/9.

Turnarounds and tritone substitution

A turnaround fills the last two bars of a tune with movement back to I: iii–vi–ii–V (or I–vi–ii–V). Make every chord a dominant 7th (E7–A7–D7–G7 in C). Then any of them can be swapped for the dominant 7th a tritone away, which has the same guide tones: E7–E♭7–D7–D♭7. The bass then slides down by half steps. Read 31.8

The same trick works on V–I alone: ♭II7 for V7. In C, the book’s example puts D♭9(13) in place of G7(♯9♯5). These two chords have the same upper notes; only the bass differs.

Listen: V7 or its tritone substitute? (Listen to the bass on the third bar.)

The blues

The book closes 31.8 with two choruses of a jazz blues, one in each kind of voicing, and points out that the voices move by step or by a 3rd. The site’s blues lessons cover the jazz blues and its substitutions with the band.

31.9 Scales

The book’s scales are for improvising: they tell a soloist which notes go with a chord. - The blues scale is the minor pentatonic with ♭5 added: 1 ♭3 4 ♭5 5 ♭7. ♭3 and ♭5 are the blue notes. The book’s example is “Sunshine of Your Love”. - The bebop dominant scale is Mixolydian with the major 7th added as a passing note going down (8 – 7 – ♭7). A first step in improvising: run it down in eighth notes from a chord tone on the downbeat. - The rest of the book’s table: the classical scales, the modes, the modes of melodic minor, and the synthetic scales (whole tone, octatonic, hexatonic). Read 31.9

31.10 Chord-scale relationships

To find a scale for a chord, write the chord’s notes (with every extension and alteration) as a scale inside an octave. Then fill the gaps, avoiding augmented 2nds and two half steps in a row. CΔ7(♯11) gives C D E F♯ G A B: Lydian. Where a chord has a minor 3rd, the gap can be filled two ways, so the book lists two scales. The key matters too. Over the opening Fm7 of “All the Things You Are” (vi7 in A♭), play F natural minor, not F Dorian: Dorian’s D♮ would clash with the key’s D♭. Read 31.10

Which scale does the book’s table give for each chord? Where it lists two, either is right:

31.11 Harmonizing the bebop scale

The book shows Mark Levine’s way (from The Jazz Theory Book) of harmonizing the bebop major scale in four parts. The tonic chord alternates with vii°7 chords in different inversions, so every passing note gets a diminished 7th. The book suggests singing each part, and points to Count Basie’s “London Bridge Is Falling Down” for a similar harmonized scale. Read 31.11

NoteListen: the book’s example

31.12 Everything together

The book’s practice exercises: 31.12. Its voice-leading exercise (five-voice close and spread voicings through a progression) needs four- and five-part writing, which this site can’t check yet.

NoteFor teachers
  • Links with your settings: open a drill’s Settings, then Copy a link with these settings. Add &lock=1 for a test, &count=20 for a score.
  • Chords: exactly the book’s Figures 31.4.1–8, on twelve roots (C D♭ D E♭ E F F♯ G A♭ A B♭ B) or the naturals. The drawn chords are stacked in thirds on a grand staff, ♯5 written as ♭6 and ♯9 as ♭10 next to a ♭7, as in the book’s figures.
  • Checking a name: the typed symbol is read by the book’s rules (31.1–31.2) and must mean the same notes over the same root, spelled as drawn (D♭9 is wrong for C♯9). A 5th the chord leaves out is fine, so C7(♯11) counts for C E G♭ B♭ (31.2). With a 5th or ♯5 present the match is exact, so C7(♭13) is wrong for C7(♯5) (31.3). C13 is wrong for C E G B♭ D A, which the book calls C9(13); “7alt” isn’t accepted as a name, since it doesn’t say which alterations.
  • Checking written notes: the root must be spelled as in the symbol; the other notes are checked by sound over the root, in any order, since the book allows respelling altered notes.
  • ii–V–I: a typed answer counts if the roots are right and the chords are of the right kind (m7-type ii, half-diminished ii in minor, any dominant V, a major- or minor-type tonic). The book’s own versions are shown as the answer.
  • The ear drill plays the book’s close voicing (root in the bass, the other notes within an octave, the 3rd or 7th lowest) on a random bass note.
  • Band demos: the band’s symbols are its own (G13 for the book’s G9(13)); its voicings are its own, not the book’s. The charts are this site’s examples of the progressions the book describes. Nobody has yet listened to check them.
  • The guide-tone example is this site’s engraving of the exercise the book describes in 31.7.1.
  • Not here: the book’s five-voice voice-leading exercise (31.12 ex. 3) and its blues choruses (31.8.3).
  • Checked: node tests/lessons/jazz-drill.test.js checks every chord and scale against tables written out separately from the book’s figures (about 89,000 checks), the chord-scale table by the book’s own principle (each chord tone is in each scale listed), and which typed answers are accepted or refused.
